Microphone guide. Only next-installment content promises logged. Product-review lines ('It will never suck', 'You won't regret it') and a quoted Schoeps marketing claim about the Colette system's future were treated as opinion or third-party marketing, not forecasts.

Reboot of Carlene MacMillan's #FreeBritney / Simone Biles essay with a short intro and postscript by the author. Body statements are hers, republished with endorsement ('This was a good article then'); own_claim kept true with notes.
Paid-subscriber audio drop plus guest bios; one own-publication plan.

Long essay on SNT (Stanford Neuromodulation Therapy, Magnus Medical) and psychiatry's communication failures. Several restatements of one SNT forecast logged separately (efficacy, regulatory status, adoption, confidence level, hedge). 'Your insurance will not currently pay for this. But it kinda should' is present-state plus normative and was not logged.
110-word intro to a joke video about the Amazon/One Medical deal; the only forward-looking wording is ironic and is logged with sincere false.

Essay on the DEA physical-office requirement ending telehealth-only business models. The R.E.M. parody lyrics ('down round', 'It's the end of the terms as we know em') restate the thesis satirically and were not logged separately. Short AI-video post; body is one line about ice cream footage and medical spend. Trailing 'Recent Posts' list is site chrome.

statements.context: Author's introduction to a republished article by his wife Carlene MacMillan: she might write for the newsletter again, conditional on subscriber growth.

statements.quote: Should she no longer have a conservator in the future, it is important to note that it won’t be smooth sailing for a celebrity in her position. Unfortunately, many of the same pressures that have haunted celebrities throughout history are not going anywhere.
statements.context: In the republished #FreeBritney essay, a conditional call: if Britney Spears's conservatorship ends, her life will not be smooth, because the pressures on celebrities persist. Setup: her father and conservator Jamie Spears faces a petition for removal.
statements.note: Text is Carlene MacMillan's original article, republished by the author with endorsement. Compound: conditional call plus persistence claim ('not going anywhere').

statements.quote: Maybe, just maybe, when Britney Spears gains full freedom to appear wherever and however she wants, she can hit the hallways of Clubhouse for the types of connected conversations that keep so many of us on their day after day.
statements.context: Closing of the republished essay: a hope that Britney Spears, once free of her conservatorship, might join Clubhouse conversations. The clause 'when Britney Spears gains full freedom' assumes the conservatorship ends.
statements.horizon_text: when Britney Spears gains full freedom
statements.note: Borderline: wish framing; the predictive content is the presupposition that Spears gains full freedom. Carlene MacMillan's text, republished with endorsement.

statements.quote: We will be releasing an edited podcast version. of this to the general public this fall
statements.context: Paid-subscriber post with the full audio of the Mental Health & NFTs Clubhouse show (August 2021); the author plans to release an edited podcast version to the general public in fall 2021.
statements.note: Own-publication plan; low forecast value. Coder may mark CONTROL. Stray period in 'version. of this' is in the source.

statements.quote: FDA Breakthrough treatments like SNT neuromodulation by Magnus Medical have the potential to relieve suffering vastly more than current treatments.
statements.context: TL;DR of the essay: Stanford Neuromodulation Therapy (SNT), an accelerated intermittent theta burst TMS protocol commercialized by Magnus Medical with FDA Breakthrough status, is expected to relieve depression far more than current treatments.
statements.note: Headline claim of the post; the detailed forecast follows ('I believe that SNT and similar approaches will demonstrate...').

statements.quote: And the “magnet therapy” research I’m about to describe, if replicated, actually meets every definition of the (transitive verb) meaning of the word cure as it applies to depression as an illness
statements.context: The author argues that the SNT ('magnet therapy', as the Today Show called it) results, if replicated, meet the dictionary definition of a cure for depression. Conditional on future replication.
statements.note: Conditional claim; replication is the future event. Definitional framing but sincere.

statements.quote: I will make further implausible claims about this treatment for depression: works in five days or less leads to remission for >50% people. doesn’t require any medication. doesn’t require talk therapy (though it may be helpful afterward). is safer than water (in that you can’t overdose) and is considered a minimal risk procedure by the FDA. lasts for months to over a year for some.
statements.context: Framed ironically as 'implausible claims' but stated sincerely: SNT works in five days or less, leads to remission for over 50% of patients, needs no medication or talk therapy, is minimal risk, and lasts for months to over a year for some. These state the Stanford study results as general properties of the treatment.
statements.note: Ironic framing around sincere assertions; existing study results stated as general properties that later replication tests. Time words in the quote describe treatment onset and duration, not a horizon.

statements.quote: SNT treatment is not yet FDA cleared, but it does have FDA Breakthrough status, which means it’s so promising that the approval process has been sped up.
statements.context: Regulatory status of SNT as of July 2022: not FDA cleared, holds Breakthrough designation; the author frames this as an accelerated path toward approval.
statements.note: Borderline: implicit expectation of eventual FDA clearance ('not yet', 'sped up'); no explicit approval call or date.

statements.quote: YES, this is a treatment that has to go through an appropriate regulatory pathway. When it is broadly offered, we will thusly understand enough about the risks and benefits to be able to offer it to the right people for the right problems at the right times.
statements.context: The author expects SNT to pass through a regulatory pathway and then be broadly offered, with enough understanding of risks and benefits by then to target it correctly.
statements.note: Presupposes SNT will be broadly offered after regulatory clearance; compound with a knowledge claim.

statements.quote: I believe that SNT and similar approaches will demonstrate both statistical significance and be—capital H—Helpful.
statements.context: Core forecast of the essay: SNT (Stanford Neuromodulation Therapy, accelerated iTBS TMS developed by Dr. Williams at Stanford) and similar approaches will show statistical significance in subsequent research and be meaningfully helpful for depression.
statements.note: Main SNT forecast; confidence level given in the following paragraph (landlord/rent analogy) and hedged afterward ('It's possible the randomized control trials won't...').

statements.quote: To make it clear for general audiences the level of faith I have in “amazing” being the outcome of subsequent research, it is near the level of faith I have that “my landlord will expect me to pay the rent next month.“
statements.context: The author quantifies his confidence that subsequent SNT research will show 'amazing' results: near certainty, compared to his landlord expecting rent next month.
statements.confidence_phrase: near the level of faith I have that “my landlord will expect me to pay the rent next month.“
statements.note: Confidence statement attached to the preceding SNT forecast; reads as a very high subjective probability.

statements.quote: It’s possible the randomized control trials won’t demonstrate the results I am expecting from having personally treated hundreds of patients with a close analog of SNT, with similar outcomes.
statements.context: Caveat to the SNT forecast: the author admits future randomized controlled trials might not replicate the results he expects, which are based on his own treatment of hundreds of patients with a close analog of SNT (accelerated iTBS).
statements.note: Hedge on the same underlying SNT forecast; also discloses that the author treats patients with a close analog (own practice interest).

statements.quote: the effort the field of psychiatry will put into sounding overly-cautious about empirically validated and wildly effective treatments will be a poor choice.
statements.context: Prediction that psychiatry as a field will communicate over-cautiously about effective new treatments like SNT, and that this will prove a poor choice, by analogy to Covid-19 vaccine messaging failures.
statements.note: Claim about field behavior; hard to resolve. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: Depression sucks, and we shouldn’t put up with it any longer than we absolutely have to. And I hope in the very near future that standard is going to be about five days
statements.context: Closing line: the author hopes and expects that in the very near future the standard time a patient must endure depression before relief will be about five days, i.e. SNT-style accelerated TMS becomes standard care.
statements.confidence_phrase: I hope ... is going to be
statements.note: Hope plus prediction; 'five days' is the SNT treatment course. First sentence is normative, second carries the forecast.

statements.quote: Therefore, I present above a video of my visionary son, who will summarize for us the true potential of this prescient acquisition.
statements.context: Joke video post on Amazon's $3.9B acquisition of One Medical (July 2022): the author's six-year-old son gives a 'hot take'. Calling the acquisition 'prescient' with 'true potential' is ironic; the sincere content is only that Amazon's brand power with children matters.
statements.note: Satirical; 'prescient acquisition' is ironic. Logged for recall only; no real expectation stated.

statements.quote: The TL;DR: With the end of the Covid-19 public health emergency, which apparently has already ended according to the DEA, there will be no telehealth-only companies anymore as we know them today.
statements.context: Headline forecast: because the DEA treats the Covid-19 public health emergency as over and requires a physical office for DEA registration (controlled-substance prescribing), telehealth-only companies such as Cerebral will not exist in their current form.
statements.horizon_text: With the end of the Covid-19 public health emergency
statements.note: Core thesis of the post; restated in the headings 'Brick and Mortar is Back in a Big Way for Healthcare' and 'Hyperscaleable Virtual-Care is Dead'.

statements.quote: The kicker: if you can’t get a medical license + DEA number, there's no credentialing with major payers! It follows that, absent a physical office in every single state for all your prescribing humans, no more national “telehealth-only” plays.
statements.context: Mechanism for the thesis: DEA registration requires a physical office in each state; without a DEA number there is no payer credentialing; therefore national telehealth-only business models cannot continue.
statements.note: Compound: present regulatory description plus forecast. Nearby: 'If they can't do this, they won't issue a new license' (DEA inspection requirement).

statements.quote: This is an expensive problem for telehealth start ups which assumed they would never, ever have to pay for any yucky offices to run their business. Good bye, capital efficiency…
statements.context: Implication of the DEA office requirement for telehealth startups: they will have to pay for physical offices, ending their capital-efficient model.
statements.note: Borderline: present cost problem with a forward implication (loss of capital efficiency).

statements.quote: Venture capital can disrupt a lot of things, but the fundamental rules around DEA licensure are not going to go down without a drawn out fight.
statements.context: Prediction that the DEA licensure rules (physical office requirement for controlled-substance prescribers) will persist; any change will need a drawn-out fight despite venture capital pressure.
statements.note: Negative call on regulatory change.

statements.quote: Stop burning money on dubious companies that don’t take concerns about patient care and liability seriously. Your portfolios will thank me.
statements.context: Advice to investors framed as a 'snarky public service message': stop funding telehealth companies that ignore patient care and liability; the predictive reading is that such investments will perform badly.
statements.note: Borderline: imperative advice with a predictive tail ('Your portfolios will thank me').

statements.quote: You could perhaps think that healthcare would go back to old working methods when restrictions were lifted?… Altogether, the emergence of the health tech/telehealth field spells a significant opportunity for tech companies and healthcare providers alike to reinvent care models that improve access, outcomes and affordability.
statements.context: Quoted from a June 1, 2022 piece by 'highly conflicted founders/authors' (telehealth ADHD care): telehealth is a significant opportunity to reinvent care models. The author rejects it ('But that was written June 1, 2022. Sorry, Bruh.'); his stance is the negation.
statements.note: Third-party forecast quoted to be rebutted; the author's stance is the opposite (telehealth-only models will end). own_claim false.

statements.quote: Hyperscaleable Virtual-Care is Dead
statements.context: Section heading: the author declares hyperscalable virtual-only care models dead, because DEA rules require physical offices and because 'There is no such thing as a huge and perfectly scalable company'.
statements.note: Negative call in a heading; restates the TL;DR thesis.

statements.quote: The hope that the conceit of investing in healthcare would be easy and wildly profitable without real innovation might—finally—have a wooden stake stabbed in is heart.
statements.context: With the DEA reasserting regulation of controlled-substance prescribing, the author hopes, with a hedge, that the venture-capital conceit of easy, scalable, wildly profitable healthcare investing without real innovation is ending.
statements.note: Hedged ('might'); framed as hope. Typo 'in is heart' is in the source.

statements.quote: Private equity does not act in the interest of patients. It’s not their job. They’re not ever going to do that.
statements.context: Footnote 11: the author asserts private equity in healthcare will never act in patients' interest, because its fiduciary duty is to investors ('don't expect scorpions not to sting').
statements.note: Negative call ('never') about a class of actors; low resolvability.
